clinicalPearls: Dense fibrous scarring that fuses the visceral and parietal pleura into a thick, often calcified peel encasing the lung
Classically follows organisation of an empyema, a haemothorax, or a long-standing exudative effusion, and may follow tuberculous pleuritis
Produces a restrictive ventilatory defect with progressive exertional breathlessness and a reduced, retracted hemithorax
Examination shows reduced chest wall movement, dull percussion, and diminished breath sounds on the affected side
Imaging demonstrates a thick, sometimes calcified pleural rind that prevents the lung from expanding to the chest wall
Decortication, surgical removal of the constricting peel, is the definitive treatment when the underlying lung is salvageable
Early drainage and clearance of empyema or haemothorax helps prevent progression to an established fibrothorax
reference.pathophysiology: When blood, pus, or a protein-rich exudate persists in the pleural space, the initial fibrinous layer becomes organised by ingrowth of fibroblasts and capillaries. Instead of resolving, the fibrin matures into dense collagenous tissue that binds the visceral and parietal pleura together as a rigid peel. This inelastic layer mechanically traps the lung, restricts expansion of the hemithorax, and impairs ventilation, and with time it may calcify. The result is a fixed restrictive defect that persists until the constricting rind is surgically removed.
additionalDifferentials: Diffuse pleural thickening from asbestos exposure
Trapped lung from an unexpandable visceral peel without generalised fibrosis
Prior tuberculous or fungal pleuritis with residual thickening
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph showing a contracted hemithorax and pleural thickening or calcification
CT of the thorax to define the extent and thickness of the pleural peel and assess the underlying lung
Pulmonary function tests confirming a restrictive pattern
MRI or ultrasound to help distinguish fibrous peel from fluid or tumour
Pleural sampling or biopsy where malignancy or ongoing infection is suspected
redFlags: Progressive breathlessness with a shrinking, immobile hemithorax
Features suggesting underlying malignancy such as an enlarging mass or bloody effusion
Signs of ongoing or recurrent pleural infection
Contralateral mediastinal shift with worsening respiratory compromise
reference.prognosis: If the trapped lung is otherwise healthy, decortication can restore substantial lung expansion and function; outcomes are poorer when there is coexisting parenchymal disease, unresolved infection, or an underlying malignancy.
pitfalls: Delaying drainage of an empyema or haemothorax until an irreversible peel has formed
Attempting decortication when the underlying lung is destroyed and cannot re-expand
Mistaking a malignant pleural process for benign post-inflammatory fibrothorax
Overlooking active infection beneath the fibrous peel before surgery
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
